intro: The second of Elgar’s “Enigma” Variations, Op. 36, an Allegro titled “H.D.S.-P.”, portrays the pianist Hew David Steuart-Powell, who ran his fingers over the keys before playing in a piano trio. Elgar turned that warm-up into a short orchestral toccata and added chromatic notes to it.

sections.label: Var 2 · Allegro, semiquaver figures in violins
sections.mNote: The violins exchange rapid semiquaver figures.

cues.title: Staccato semiquavers, violins
cues.text: The first violins begin a staccato run, and the seconds take it up. Sharps and naturals crowd the short figures, which parody a pianist’s warm-up exercise. The woodwinds follow.
cues.evidence: Novello full score, p. 8, rehearsal 5: semiquaver exchanges between the violin sections, followed by woodwinds. Elgar explains the parody in his commentary on variation II, reproduced at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Piano trio partners of Elgar
cues.text: H.D.S.-P. played piano trios with Elgar on violin and Basil Nevinson on cello. Elgar gave each of them a variation. The pianist’s is this Allegro, and the cellist’s is the twelfth variation, which has a long cello solo.
cues.evidence: The Elgar Society identifies the trio and the subjects of variations II and XII: https://elgar.org/3enigma.htm. Novello full score, pp. 8 and 82.

source.title: Elgar, Enigma Variations, full score (Novello)
source.locator: Novello full score, pp. 8–14, rehearsal figures 5–7: violin semiquavers, woodwind replies and the closing flute and clarinet solos.

timeline.note: The two violin sections pass staccato semiquavers between them (p. 8).
Woodwinds answer the running string figures (pp. 8–9).
Wind accents punctuate the quick string phrases (pp. 10–11).
Flutes and clarinets answer while the strings alternate running notes and shorter replies (p. 12).
A solo timpani figure enters under the last violin exchanges and the quiet wind replies (pp. 13–14).
The running violins stop; short flute and clarinet solos finish over the lower strings (p. 14).

composer.epithet: Composer of the Enigma Variations, a set of variations drawn from his friendships, who also recorded his own music for the gramophone.
facts: His father’s Worcester music shop; violin and organ; composition largely self-taught
Powick bandmaster, instrumental teacher and organist at St George’s, Worcester
Two symphonies; violin and cello concertos; Gerontius; five Pomp and Circumstance marches
Master of the King’s Musick from 1924; recordings of his own orchestral works
composer.background:
Elgar grew up among the instruments and sheet music in his father’s Worcester shop. William tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church; Edward studied the scores, learned several instruments and earned money with his violin. Born at Lower Broadheath on 2 June 1857, he had hoped to study at Leipzig, but the family could not afford it. Playing in the Three Choirs Festival orchestra, he learned the choral music of Handel and Mendelssohn as a member of the string section.

From 1879 to 1884 he was bandmaster at Worcester County Asylum, Powick. He trained members of staff to play for the patients and supplied quadrilles and polkas for the Friday-evening dances. He knew each player in this orchestra individually and had to write within their capabilities. He also taught in local schools and gave private lessons in Malvern. In 1885 he succeeded William at the organ of St George’s.
